average rate of change: The change in a function's output divided by the change in input over an interval, equal to the secant line's slope.
complex conjugate: For a number a+bi, the partner a−bi; multiplying the two yields a real number.
complex number: A number of the form a+bi, where a is the real part and b is the imaginary part.
complex zero: A complex value of the variable that makes a polynomial equal to zero.
composite function: A function formed by applying one function to the output of another, written (f∘g)(x)=f(g(x)).
concavity: The direction a graph curves, upward or downward, determined by how its rate of change is changing.
conjugate root theorem: For a polynomial with real coefficients, complex roots always occur in conjugate pairs.
critical value: A boundary value, such as a zero, where the sign of an expression may change.
cross: Passing through the x-axis with a sign change, which happens at zeros of odd multiplicity.
degree: The highest exponent in a polynomial, which determines its end behavior and number of zeros.
domain: The set of all input x-values for which a function is defined, excluding values that make a denominator zero.
end behavior: How a function's output behaves as x approaches positive or negative infinity, governed by the leading term.
extrapolation: Using a model to predict values beyond the range of the original data, which should be done cautiously.
factor theorem: The theorem stating that f(r)=0 if and only if (x−r) is a factor of f(x).
factoring over ℂ: Completely splitting a polynomial into a product of linear factors using complex numbers.
factoring over ℝ: Splitting a polynomial into a product of linear and quadratic factors with real coefficients.
finite differences: The differences between consecutive outputs at equally spaced inputs, used to gauge a polynomial's degree.
fundamental theorem of algebra: Every polynomial of degree n has exactly n zeros when counted over the complex numbers.
goodness of fit: A measure of how well a model describes or matches a set of data.
hole: A removable discontinuity at an x-value where a common factor cancels in a rational function.
horizontal asymptote: A horizontal line a function approaches as x goes to positive or negative infinity, found by comparing degrees.
horizontal line test: A test stating a function is one-to-one if every horizontal line meets its graph at most once.
imaginary unit: The number i, defined by the property i²=−1.
inner function: In a composition, the function g that is applied first.
instantaneous rate of change: The rate of change at a single point, the limit of average rates and equal to the tangent line's slope.
intercept: A point where a graph meets a coordinate axis, either an x-intercept or a y-intercept.
interval notation: A notation for sets of numbers where parentheses exclude endpoints and brackets include them.
inverse function: A function f⁻¹ that undoes the action of f, so that f⁻¹(f(x))=x.
leading term: The term of highest degree in a polynomial, which dominates its end behavior.
long division: A polynomial division procedure used to find the quotient, including for slant asymptotes.
modeling: The process of approximating real data with a function or equation.
multiplicity: The number of times a factor (x−r) is repeated, determining whether the graph crosses or touches the axis.
oblique/slant asymptote: A slanted asymptote that occurs when the numerator's degree is exactly one greater than the denominator's.
one-to-one function: A function in which different inputs always give different outputs, the condition for an inverse to exist.
outer function: In a composition, the function f that is applied second.
parameter: An adjustable coefficient or constant in a model equation.
parent function: The simplest base function before transformations; for rational functions it is 1/x.
polynomial division: The procedure of dividing one polynomial by another to find a quotient and remainder.
polynomial function: A function that is a sum of terms with non-negative integer exponents.
polynomial inequality: An inequality such as f(x)>0 or f(x)<0 that asks about the sign of a polynomial.
range: The set of all output values a function actually produces.
rate of change: How much a function's output changes as the independent variable changes, measured by slope.
rational function: A function written as the ratio of two polynomials, P(x)/Q(x).
real part: The value a in the complex number a+bi.
real root: A zero of a function where the graph actually meets the x-axis.
reflection: A transformation that flips a graph across an axis.
regression: A statistical procedure for finding the function parameters that best fit a set of data.
remainder theorem: The theorem stating the remainder when f(x) is divided by (x−r) equals f(r).
removable discontinuity: A discontinuity at a single missing point, shown as an open circle on the graph.
residual: The difference between an observed value and the value predicted by a model, used to check fit.
secant line: A straight line through two points on a curve, whose slope is the average rate of change.
second differences: The differences of the first differences in an equally spaced table, whose sign indicates concavity.
sign chart: A table organizing the sign of an expression on each interval determined by its zeros.
solution set: The set of all x-values that satisfy an inequality, often expressed in interval notation.
stretch/compression: A transformation that lengthens or shortens a graph by a coefficient factor.
synthetic division: A fast shortcut for dividing a polynomial by (x−r) using only its coefficients.
tangent line: A line that just touches a curve at one point, whose slope is the instantaneous rate of change.
test value: An arbitrary value chosen within an interval to determine the sign of an expression there.
touch/bounce: Touching the x-axis and turning back without crossing, which happens at zeros of even multiplicity.
translation/shift: A transformation that moves a graph horizontally or vertically.
vertical asymptote: An x-value where the denominator is zero after canceling, causing the function to diverge to ±∞.
zero / root: An x-value where f(x)=0, the point at which the graph meets the x-axis.
back-conversion: Converting a logarithmic value back through exponentiation to recover the original quantity.
change of base for exponentials: Rewriting b^x as e^(x ln b) to express any exponential with base e.
change of base formula: The formula log_b x = ln x / ln b, allowing any-base logarithms to be computed.
common logarithm: A logarithm with base 10, written log x.
constant difference: The hallmark of linear data, in which the absolute change is the same each step.
constant ratio: The hallmark of exponential data, in which the multiplicative ratio is the same each step.
continuous compounding: Growth that compounds continuously, given by the formula A=Pe^(rt).
decibel: A logarithmic scale for sound intensity, defined by dB=10 log(I/I₀).
decay factor: A base b between 0 and 1, causing the function value to shrink each unit step.
domain restriction: The requirement that the argument of a logarithm must be positive.
effective annual rate: The actual fractional growth over one year; for continuous rate r it is e^r−1.
euler's number e: The irrational number about 2.718, the natural base of continuous growth.
exponential decay: A decrease in function value that occurs when the base satisfies 0<b<1.
exponential equation: An equation in which the unknown appears in an exponent.
exponential function: A function of the form f(x)=ab^x that changes by a constant multiple per unit increase in x.
exponential growth: An accelerating increase in function value that occurs when the base b>1.
exponential model: A model of data using the form y=ab^x.
extraneous solution: A value produced during solving that does not actually satisfy the original equation.
growth factor: The multiple b applied per unit of x; values greater than 1 produce growth.
horizontal shift: A transformation moving a graph left or right, produced by replacing x with (x−h).
identity: The function that returns its input unchanged, the result of composing inverse functions.
initial value: The function value a when x=0.
inverse relationship: A relationship in which two functions each undo the other's action.
linearization: Transforming curved data into a straight line, often using logarithms.
log-log plot: A graph with both axes on logarithmic scales, which straightens power functions.
logarithm: The inverse operation of exponentiation: log_b(x)=y means b^y=x.
logarithm properties: Rules that turn products into sums, quotients into differences, and powers into coefficients.
logarithmic function: The function log_b x, with positive domain and a range of all real numbers.
logarithmic regression: Fitting saturating growth with a model of the form y=a+b ln x.
logarithmic scale: An axis on which each step represents a multiplicative factor rather than an additive one.
matching to graph: Pairing an equation with its graph using clues like asymptotes, intercepts, and growth behavior.
model selection: Choosing the type of function that best fits the pattern in a set of data.
natural exponential function: The exponential function with base e, written e^x.
natural logarithm: A logarithm with base e, written ln x.
nominal rate: The stated interest rate r that does not account for compounding frequency.
percent change: The percentage change in function value per unit of x, equal to (b−1)×100%.
periodic compounding: Compounding at fixed intervals, given by A=P(1+r/n)^(nt).
ph scale: A logarithmic acidity scale defined by pH=−log[H⁺], where each unit lower is ten times more acidic.
power function: A function of the form y=ax^n.
ratio: A multiplicative comparison of two quantities, central to comparisons on a logarithmic scale.
recovering parameters: Computing a, b, or n back from the slope and intercept of a linearized line.
reflection over y=x: The symmetry between the graphs of a function and its inverse.
richter scale: A logarithmic scale for earthquake magnitude, where each unit difference is ten times the amplitude.
semi-log plot: A graph with only the y-axis on a logarithmic scale, which straightens exponential data.
vertical shift: A transformation moving a graph up or down by adding k, which also moves the asymptote.
vertical stretch: A transformation lengthening or shrinking a graph by a coefficient a.
amplitude: The distance |A| from the midline to a maximum or minimum of a periodic graph.
angular frequency: The coefficient B that sets the period, where period equals 2π/B.
arc length: The length of an arc on a circle, given by s=rθ with θ in radians.
arccosine: The inverse cosine function, arccos x, with range [0, π].
arcsine: The inverse sine function, arcsin x, with range [−π/2, π/2].
arctangent: The inverse tangent function, arctan x, with range (−π/2, π/2).
cardioid: A heart-shaped polar curve of the form r=a(1±cosθ).
composition: Applying a trigonometric function and an inverse trigonometric function in sequence.
cosecant: The reciprocal of sine, cscθ=1/sinθ, with range |y|≥1.
cosine: The x-coordinate of a point on the unit circle, written cosθ.
cotangent: The ratio cotθ=cosθ/sinθ, with asymptotes where sinθ=0.
cycle: One complete repetition of a periodic graph.
double-angle formula: A formula expressing functions of 2θ, such as sin2θ and cos2θ, in terms of a single angle.
equivalent rewriting: Changing the form of an expression without changing its value.
factorable equation: A trigonometric equation solved by treating the trig ratio as a variable and factoring.
general solution: The set of all solutions to a trig equation, expressed by adding multiples of the period.
half-angle formula: A formula expressing trig functions of θ/2 in terms of functions of θ.
identity proof: Showing two sides are equal by transforming one side into the other.
inverse trig function: A function that returns the angle producing a given trigonometric ratio.
limaçon: A polar curve of the form r=a±bcosθ.
midline: The horizontal center line y=D of a sinusoidal graph.
parameter interpretation: Interpreting the constants A, B, C, and D of a model in terms of a real situation.
period: The horizontal length 2π/B over which one cycle of a function repeats.
phase shift: The horizontal shift C of a sinusoidal graph.
polar angle θ: The angle θ measured from the positive x-axis in polar coordinates.
polar coordinates: A coordinate system locating points by a distance r and an angle θ.
pole: The origin of the polar coordinate system, reached when r=0 regardless of θ.
principal value: The single inverse-function value selected by restricting the range.
pythagorean identity: The identity sin²θ+cos²θ=1 and its variations.
quadrantal angle: An angle lying on an axis, such as 0, π/2, π, or 3π/2.
radial distance r: The distance r from the pole to a point in polar coordinates.
radian: A unit of angle defined as the ratio of arc length to radius.
reference angle: The acute angle a terminal side makes with the x-axis, setting the magnitude of trig values.
rose curve: A petal-shaped polar curve of the form r=a cos(nθ).
secant: The reciprocal of cosine, secθ=1/cosθ, with range |y|≥1.
sine: The y-coordinate of a point on the unit circle, written sinθ.
sinusoidal model: A model fitting periodic data with the form y=A sin(B(x−C))+D.
solutions on interval: All solutions to an equation within a given range such as [0, 2π).
sum/difference formula: A formula for trig functions of a sum or difference of angles, such as sin(α±β).
symmetry test: A test for whether a polar graph is symmetric about the polar axis, the pole, or θ=π/2.
tangent: The ratio tanθ=sinθ/cosθ, with asymptotes where cosθ=0.
trig identity: A trigonometric equation that holds true for every angle.
trigonometric equation: An equation that contains trigonometric functions.
unit circle: The circle of radius 1 centered at the origin, the basis for defining trig functions.
arithmetic sequence: A sequence in which the common difference d between consecutive terms is constant.
augmented matrix: A coefficient matrix with the constant column attached, written [A|b].
bearing: A compass direction measured from north or south, which must be converted to a standard angle.
cartesian form: The equation of a curve expressed using only x and y.
common difference: The constant difference d between consecutive terms of an arithmetic sequence.
common ratio: The constant ratio r between consecutive terms of a geometric sequence.
completing the square: Rewriting a quadratic into the form (x−h)² plus a constant.
components: The horizontal and vertical parts of a vector, written ⟨a,b⟩.
conditional probability: The probability of A given B, P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B).
conic section: A curve formed by slicing a cone with a plane: circle, ellipse, parabola, or hyperbola.
convergence: The behavior of a series whose sum approaches a finite value, occurring when |r|<1.
cramer's rule: A method giving xᵢ=det(Aᵢ)/det(A), valid only when det(A)≠0.
determinant: A single number associated with a square matrix; for a 2×2 matrix it is ad−bc.
dimensions: The number of rows and columns of a matrix, written m×n.
direction angle: The angle a vector makes with the positive x-axis, found from arctan(b/a).
directrix: The fixed line used in the geometric definition of a parabola.
divergence: The behavior of a series whose sum does not approach a single value, occurring when |r|≥1.
dot product: The scalar u·v=u₁v₁+u₂v₂=|u||v|cosθ formed from two vectors.
eccentricity: A value e measuring how much a conic deviates from a circle, determining its type.
eliminating the parameter: Removing t to convert parametric equations into a single Cartesian equation in x and y.
empirical rule: The rule that about 68%, 95%, and 99.7% of normal data lie within 1, 2, and 3 standard deviations.
focus: A fixed point used to define a conic section.
gaussian elimination: A method that uses row operations to reduce a matrix to row echelon form.
general form: The equation of a conic written as Ax²+By²+Cx+Dy+E=0.
geometric sequence: A sequence in which the common ratio r between consecutive terms is constant.
identity matrix: A matrix I with ones on the diagonal and zeros elsewhere.
infinite geometric series: The sum of infinitely many terms of a geometric sequence.
infinitely many solutions: A dependent system that has free variables and thus infinitely many solutions.
inverse matrix: A matrix A⁻¹ with AA⁻¹=I, which exists when det(A)≠0.
matrix multiplication: A product defined by taking dot products of rows with columns.
net force: The single vector sum of several forces.
no solution: An inconsistent system, signaled by a row stating 0 equals a nonzero constant.
non-commutativity: The property that, in general, AB≠BA for matrices.
normal distribution: A symmetric bell-shaped distribution centered on its mean.
orientation: The direction in which a parametric curve is traced as t increases.
parametric equations: Equations x=x(t) and y=y(t) that express a curve through a parameter.
reduced row echelon form: The standard matrix form from which solutions can be read directly.
relative velocity: Velocity measured with respect to a moving frame, found as a vector difference.
resolving into components: Breaking a vector into its horizontal and vertical parts.
resultant: The vector resulting from adding several vectors together.
row operations: Allowed transformations of a matrix: swapping rows, scaling a row, or adding rows.
scalar multiplication: Multiplying each component of a vector by a number to change its size or direction.
scatter plot: A statistical graph showing the relationship between two variables as plotted points.
sequence: An ordered list of numbers following a rule.
series: The sum of the terms of a sequence.
skew: The degree to which a distribution leans to one side rather than being symmetric.
standard angle: An angle measured counterclockwise from the positive x-axis.
standard deviation: A measure σ of how spread out data is from the mean.
standard form: An organized equation form from which a conic's center, axes, and foci can be read directly.
trace: The curve a point traces out as the parameter t varies.
unique solution: A system with exactly one solution, occurring when det(A)≠0.
unit vector: A vector of magnitude 1, v/|v|, indicating only direction.
vector: A quantity that has both magnitude and direction.
vector addition: Adding vectors component by component to produce a resultant vector.
vertex: The endpoint where a conic's major axis meets the curve.
